In a study of 10 technology domains (50,000 more patents), we find that a domain's classification breadth--the number of distinct CPC subgroups spanned--predicts approach performance (Pearson r=-0.642, p=0.045, N=10), and that patents per subgroup is an even stronger predictor (r=0.715, p=0.020). This provides a checkable signal for practitioners to determine where the method is most valuable. We report all findings with statistical transparency and release a complete, 91-test automated implementation.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Evaluating LLM Creativity through Long-Tail Performance
item.description: arXiv:2610.12998v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Creativity benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) vary widely in task and metric design. This raises the question of whether they capture a common notion of creativity. We propose that this shared target can be formalized as task-specific performance in the long tail of a reference input-output distribution, which describes how common input-output pairs are relative to a chosen source of text. We ground this proposition in the novelty-quality product formulation and evaluate it empirically across 15 benchmarks and 26 open-weight models, using n-gram absence from the pretraining data as a novelty proxy. Our results show that creativity benchmarks lie further in the tail regions than standard benchmarks. Moreover, on both creativity and standard benchmarks, model rankings from higher-tail subsets of each benchmark align more closely with human creativity judgments in LM-Arena. Building on these findings, we introduce q@Tail($\alpha$), a lower-cost creativity diagnostic that measures mean task quality on the tail fraction of an existing benchmark. Applying it to creativity-promoting methods reveals substantial room to improve LLM creativity through stronger tail performance.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Hindsight Structured Advice Distillation: Steering Executor Agents with Advisors Trained on Their Failures and Task Characteristics
item.description: arXiv:2610.13000v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language-model agents are used for specialized work such as financial research, healthcare and law. Such agents are often capable enough for a task but still miss its details. In finance, for example, these details include which filing reports a figure or how a company discloses a metric. Retraining the agent to learn these details is expensive, and often impossible when the agent is a closed or shared system. Writing the missing know-how into the agent's prompt makes the prompt long and identical for every input, although different inputs need different guidance. We propose to learn to generate this guidance instead. A small advisor model reads each input and writes structured advice, which is appended to the prompt of a frozen executor. The advisor is trained with hindsight, following work on distillation with privileged information. On a training pool with graded answers, we analyse the executor's failures, run it under several strategies to see which one worked on each input, and let a teacher that sees the grades and the traces write the advice that would have helped. The advisor then learns, by supervised fine-tuning, to write that advice from the input alone. Because the student is a separate small model rather than the executor, it is cheap to train and adds little latency. We call this approach hindsight structured advice distillation (HSAD). On FrontierFinance, a public benchmark of expert-written financial research queries, an 8B advisor raises the qualification rate of Samaya's proprietary research agent, which already leads the benchmark's leaderboard, from 52.9% to 56.6%. This is above the agent's own high-effort configuration, at 37% lower cost per query. We study the generalization of the proposed approach, and in particular show that HSAD also improves results on WebShop, BIRD text-to-SQL and ExpertLongBench.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] SlackSwap: Bandwidth-Aware Activation Swapping and Recomputation for Memory-Efficient DNN Training
item.description: arXiv:2610.13003v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Swapping saved activations to host memory once enabled GPUs to train models that exceeded their device-memory capacity when compute throughput and host-link bandwidth were roughly balanced. For example, on a 2015 Titan X, PCIe bandwidth was sufficient to offload all VGG-16 activations during the forward pass. This balance no longer holds. From the Titan X to the H100, peak training throughput increased by 141x, whereas host-link bandwidth improved by only 3.9x. On an A100, the host link can hide transfers for only 11-38% of the activations in the transformer models we study. Existing swapping approaches, such as vDNN, SuperNeurons, and SwapAdvisor, offload tensors according to memory requirements without explicitly respecting the available link-time budget, resulting in transfer-induced stalls; block checkpointing, in contrast, leaves the host link underutilized. We present SlackSwap, which treats host-link time as an explicit resource budget. Using a single profiled iteration, SlackSwap allocates the forward-pass link budget to tensors that are most expensive to recompute, resolves the remaining memory deficit by recomputing the least expensive tensors, and schedules FIFO offloads and earliest-deadline-first prefetches without per-layer synchronization barriers. In trace-driven simulations of BERT-Large, GPT-2 XL, and a Llama-7B-style model on an A100, SlackSwap retains 96-100% of unlimited-memory GPU throughput while using half the activation memory, achieving 1.10-1.11x the throughput of the best baseline. Its plans are within 0.5% of a genetic search over 6,600-14,000 candidate plans, while requiring less than 0.4 seconds to generate.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] CeDR-Nav: Cross-Embodiment Mapless Navigation via Offline Demonstration Recasting
item.description: arXiv:2610.13007v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Learning-based methods have demonstrated strong performance in mapless robot navigation. However, a learned policy remains restricted to the embodiment on which it was trained. Many cross-embodiment navigation methods require time-consuming online training and can still underperform target-specific policies. In fact, demonstrations collected on a source embodiment already contain navigation experience that is potentially reusable for deriving a policy for each target embodiment, but the embodiment mismatch prevents these demonstrations from directly serving as valid supervision for the target. In this article, we present CeDR-Nav, a cross-embodiment demonstration recasting framework that trains a dedicated navigation policy for each target embodiment from existing source demonstrations without online data collection. Geometry-consistent scaling with per-demonstration validity assessment converts the source demonstrations into target training data, and a target-specific Gaussian mixture policy generates feasible avoidance maneuvers for each target embodiment. Extensive quantitative simulations and real-world deployments across multiple robot platforms demonstrate the effectiveness of CeDR-Nav, with an average success-rate gain of 13.8 percentage points over DRL-DCLP in cross-embodiment simulations and target-specific policy training completed within seconds.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Provenance-Aware Belief Updating in Human-AI Feedback Loops
item.description: arXiv:2610.13008v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In repeated human-AI interaction, a single observation can be quoted, summarized, and returned to a model as multiple reports, making repetition look like independent corroboration. We study whether language models can use supplied report lineage to update according to evidence provenance rather than report count. We introduce Latent Quotient Evidence Training (LQET), a relational objective that combines sparse Bayesian supervision with constraints that encourage stable predictions when reports add no new evidence and consistent updates to the same new evidence across relay histories. On a controlled binary benchmark, LQET reduces new-evidence update RMSE by 41-44% and log-odds drift after eight relay steps by 89-91% relative to task-only training across Qwen3-4B and Phi-4-mini, with three paired training seeds per backbone. The gains extend to a closed-loop simulation in which model confidence controls how many relayed reports re-enter the model's context in later rounds. By grounding belief updates in supplied provenance, LQET offers a route toward dynamic human-AI systems in which influence follows new evidence, not the number of times the same evidence returns.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Minimizing fuzzy Kripke models over residuated lattices
item.description: arXiv:2610.13010v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Model minimization is a fundamental problem in formal methods, as smaller models can substantially reduce the complexity of model analysis and reasoning while preserving relevant semantic properties. This work studies the minimization of finite fuzzy Kripke models over residuated lattices while preserving global or local assertions in fuzzy modal logics, which are either fuzzy propositional dynamic logic or a restriction thereof, optionally enriched with nominals, converse modalities, and/or the universal program constructor. We prove that, whenever the multiplication operator of the underlying residuated lattice is right-continuous, the quotient model induced by the greatest fuzzy auto-bisimulation is a minimal reduction preserving global assertions. If the underlying fuzzy modal logic includes the universal program constructor, this quotient model is also a minimal reduction preserving local assertions and a minimal fuzzy Kripke model bisimilar to the original model. In the case where the universal program constructor is absent and the multiplication operator is additionally strictly monotone with respect to~1, we present the first algorithm for constructing a minimal reduction preserving local assertions; the resulting model is also a minimal bisimilar model.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Learning Features, Not Layouts: Feature-Axis Attention as a Transfer Prior for Medical Imaging
item.description: arXiv:2610.13012v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Natural-image-pretrained foundation models are increasingly adapted to medical imaging, yet transfer remains unreliable under domain shift, modality heterogeneity, and label scarcity. We trace part of this fragility to an overlooked design choice. Standard vision transformers place all global modeling on self-attention over spatial tokens, an object-layout prior well suited to natural scenes but not to medical images, where the discriminative signal lies in feature correlations and texture that recur across scanners while layout does not. We ask whether the axis of global attention, spatial versus feature, is itself a lever for transferable medical representations. Existing channel-aware hybrids confound this question, adding channel attention to a spatially-mixed backbone and leaving the axes coupled and the feature axis unmeasurable in isolation. We design FAD-ViT, a backbone that strictly decouples the two axes, making feature-axis attention the primary global operator and the attention axis a controlled variable. Evaluating comprehensively across 23 classification, segmentation, and low-data tasks under matched tokenization, capacity, and protocol, we find that shifting global attention from the spatial to the feature axis leaves from-scratch performance essentially unchanged, yet markedly strengthens transfer. Identical ImageNet pretraining yields up to roughly three times the transfer gain, with consistent improvements on every held-out segmentation task at up to a quarter the parameter count and far lower compute than standard and channel-attention baselines. The advantage is largest where texture rather than geometry is discriminative, tracking greater reuse of pretrained features. The axis of global attention is thus a design lever for medical transfer, and making it channel-primary is a simple, cheap, and principled choice.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Evidential Multimodal Transformers with Dempster-Shafer Fusion for Emotion Recognition
item.description: arXiv:2610.13013v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Softmax-based multimodal emotion recognition methods often assign high confidence even when sensor data are corrupted or contradictory, for example when facial expressions suggest positive valence while vocal prosody indicates negative arousal. We present an Evidential Multimodal Transformer with Dempster-Shafer Fusion (EMT-DS) that addresses this problem through formal uncertainty quantification. EMT-DS models predictions as Subjective Opinions (Dirichlet distributions), separating epistemic uncertainty (lack of evidence) from aleatoric uncertainty (sensor noise). Modality-specific transformer encoders produce belief mass distributions that are fused with Dempster's Rule of Combination, which normalizes the joint belief mass by a conflict coefficient 1/(1-c), so that contradictory evidence is explicitly quantified as conflict and the fused prediction becomes diffuse rather than being forced into an unjustified consensus. Under subject-independent and speaker-independent evaluation on four benchmarks, EMT-DS achieves 84.3% accuracy on IEMOCAP versus 81.7% for the best baseline (p < 0.01), 82.4% on DEAP under leave-one-subject-out evaluation versus 78.1%, and 96.8% on the highly imbalanced KEMDy20, and it improves accuracy on CMU-MOSEI by 2.4 points over the strongest evidential baseline. In controlled ablation, it reduces Expected Calibration Error from 0.153 (softmax transformer) to 0.042. It maintains 71.2% accuracy under severe Gaussian noise on audio features (sigma = 1.0), where attention baselines drop to 45.3%, and degrades gracefully when entire modalities are absent. The fusion step has O(MK^2) complexity, compared with O(M^2 d^2) for cross-modal attention. The learned conflict metric also flags likely errors: reviewing 20% of samples captures 80% of misclassifications, which supports selective prediction in clinical and safety-critical systems.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Generalized Proximal Policy Optimization: Unifying LLM RL Algorithms from the Perspective of Divergence
item.description: arXiv:2610.13015v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning has become the foundational paradigm for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of LLMs. Yet the dominant approach, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), relies on a geometrically degenerate clipping proxy that cannot adapt its resistance to policy shifts, leading to premature clipping and degraded exploration. Subsequent variants alleviate these issues through fragmented and heuristic modifications. We propose Generalized Proximal Policy Optimization (GPPO), a principled and unified framework for understanding and designing LLM RL algorithms through the lens of divergence. We establish a generalized $f$-divergence trust-region theory with a monotonic performance improvement guarantee, and show that different $f$-divergences induce distinct geometries and policy update dynamics. We further introduce novel estimator topologies that provide more faithful divergence estimates than the conventional single-sample Monte Carlo estimation. Under this framework, PPO and recent variants such as DAPO, DPPO, and RIPO emerge as special cases, establishing a principled two-dimensional design space of {Divergence $\times$ Estimator}. Extensive experiments on eight competition-level math and coding benchmarks show that both dimensions are critical. The best-performing GPPO instantiation surpasses standard GRPO by up to 50% and 14% on math and coding, delivering SOTA performance.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Trajectory-Aware Policy Optimization: Closing the State Distribution Gap in Long-Horizon LLM RL
item.description: arXiv:2610.13020v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a dominant paradigm for enhancing LLMs' reasoning capabilities. Yet long-horizon autoregressive rollouts introduce a fundamental limitation: local policy mismatch can compound into severe state distribution shift over trajectories. Existing LLM RL methods, such as GRPO and GSPO, control policy mismatch at the token or sequence level, but overlook this trajectory-induced shift, causing training instability and eventual collapse as the horizon grows. To close the state distribution gap, we propose Trajectory-Aware Policy Optimization (TAPO), a principled framework that theoretically derives the state-distribution correction from the off-policy policy gradient and incorporates it into the RL objective. TAPO further employs a geometric-mean estimator for variance reduction, together with a length-aware dynamic clipping that prevents overly deviated updates across the trajectory. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TAPO significantly surpasses existing LLM RL algorithms across eight competition-level benchmarks, achieving up to 48% and 12% improvement over GRPO on mathematical reasoning and algorithmic coding, with substantially enhanced training stability.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] EmbodiedCLBench: Evaluating Continual Learning for Self-Evolving Embodied Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.13021v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continual learning requires models to accumulate past experience and transfer it to new tasks. Despite substantial research on continual learning, existing work remains largely confined to non-embodied settings, without extending to embodied environments. To address this gap, we introduce EmbodiedCLBench, the first benchmark in embodied simulation for evaluating the continual learning capability of self-evolving agents. With compositional generalization as the core evaluation principle, our benchmark evaluates whether agents can first learn from basic tasks and then recombine the acquired skills to solve complex, unseen advanced tasks. Based on EmbodiedCLBench, we conduct extensive experiments across multiple agent harnesses and learning methods, revealing consistent limitations and distinctive behaviors. Our results show that while advanced tasks can be hardly solved under zero-shot setting, the experience from basic tasks enables consistent improvement. Such benefit from the experience remains stable even if the task complexity increases. However, this improvement does not scale accordingly with the number of learning samples, and current agents cannot extract meaningful information from additional experience. Collectively, our findings highlight continual learning as a fundamental yet underexplored capability, and our benchmark offers valuable resources for designing effective self-evolving agents in embodied environments. Our code and dataset are available at https://pku-value-lab.github.io/EmbodiedCLBench-homepage.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Don't Guess, Just Ask: Evaluating Interactive Requirement Clarification for Repository-Level Software Development
item.description: arXiv:2610.13022v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As LLMs become increasingly capable of implementing software, a critical bottleneck emerges: whether they truly understand what users want. Users often begin with vague intent, leaving important requirements to be clarified through interaction. In repository-level development, misunderstandings can propagate and cause costly rework. However, existing benchmarks typically evaluate implementation from complete specifications or underspecified requests, overlooking pre-coding requirement clarification. Prior clarification studies mainly focus on function-level tasks. It therefore remains unclear how well LLMs can transform vague intent into clear requirements through interaction and how this capability affects subsequent code generation. We introduce ReqClarifyBench, an interactive requirement clarification benchmark for repository-level software development. It contains 341 tasks spanning game, miniapp, and web development, each with a vague user intent, a human-validated requirement document, and code evaluation artifacts. We employ LLM-based user simulators with diverse personas derived from real-world conversations. We evaluate six LLMs in terms of clarification effectiveness and generated requirement document quality. Results show that stronger clarification effectiveness does not necessarily translate into higher document quality, and performance varies substantially across user personas. We also find that coding-agent harnesses do not further improve requirement document quality compared with their base LLMs. These findings offer insights for building LLM-based end-to-end software development systems.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Unified Generative Video Compression with Autoregressive and Bidirectional Video Diffusion
item.description: arXiv:2610.13023v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Video diffusion models can reconstruct visually compelling content from severely compressed representations at ultra-low bitrates, but they impose a rigid deployment trade-off. Bidirectional (BI) models achieve high quality through dense full-sequence attention, yet require the entire sequence before reconstruction and incur substantial latency. Autoregressive (AR) models enable low-delay streaming, but their restricted temporal context reduces compression efficiency. This tension is particularly relevant when a video stream must be decoded in real time yet is also stored for later, quality-oriented playback, making AR and BI models natural choices for the live and replay stages, respectively. To support both stages, we present UniGVC, a Unified Generative Video Codec that supports two decoding modes from a single bitstream. UniGVC-BI employs a BI-DiT with dense attention for quality-oriented random-access decoding, whereas UniGVC-AR uses windowed AR-DiT for low-delay streaming. Both paths share a hierarchical latent codec that recurrently produces the same conditions with ultra-low bitrates, allowing UniGVC-BI to serve as a conditional teacher for single-step distillation of UniGVC-AR. A tiny conditional video decoder further reduces streaming latency while preserving most of the reconstruction quality. On standard 1080p benchmarks, UniGVC-BI achieves the best overall rate-distortion-perception trade-off among the evaluated methods and produces temporally stable video at rates as low as 0.0005 bits per pixel. Meanwhile, UniGVC-AR remains competitive while decoding 1080p video at 36.85 FPS, over $250\times$ faster than UniGVC-BI. Code and models will be released later.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] What Visual Representations Do World Action Models Need?
item.description: arXiv:2610.13024v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) inherit powerful priors from pretrained video generation models, but their variational autoencoder (VAE) representations are optimized for visual reconstruction rather than manipulation. External visual representations can improve manipulation, but existing methods couple representation choices with different integration mechanisms, obscuring their individual effects. We systematically compare visual representations, five integration mechanisms, and feature combinations under controlled settings. Our study yields three main findings. First, strong general-purpose visual representations provide broader robustness gains and can match or outperform representations pretrained for specific visual capabilities. Second, channel-wise joint prediction achieves the highest average success rate; further analyses suggest that future-feature prediction and the action expert's effective use of added visual information contribute to its gains. Third, additional sources should be selected for the task-relevant information they contribute beyond existing representations, as the same source can help one combination but harm another. However, even the best evaluated composition provides a smaller additional gain than the initial improvement from adding a strong general-purpose representation to the VAE-only baseline. We instantiate the resulting Representation Recipe as R$^2$-WAM. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on RoboCasa GR1 Tabletop with an 84.7% success rate and reaches 92.8% on RoboTwin 2.0, improving over the VAE-only baselines by 5.9 and 2.2 percentage points, respectively. Taken together, these findings suggest that future work should prioritize stronger general-purpose visual representations and more effective mechanisms for integrating them into WAMs, with feature composition serving as a supplementary route to improvement.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Evo$^2$: Evolving the Evolver through Weight-Harness Co-Evolution
item.description: arXiv:2610.13025v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-evolving agents are increasingly used to improve language model systems without human intervention through either weight updates or harness improvements. Existing approaches typically pursue these directions separately: some methods update model weights using self-generated experience, while others rewrite the harness that defines how an agent uses prompts, tools, context, and execution feedback. However, these approaches overlook the relationship between model weights and the agent harness. To connect these processes and ensure effective and smooth agent self-evolving, we propose Evo$^2$, a framework for weight-harness co-evolution. For harness updates, we design a unified dual-role pipeline that a single policy serves as both a Proposer, which writes harness edits, and a Reflector, which diagnoses their effects and guides revision. For weight updates, harness modifications and their execution outcomes guide the training of both the Proposer and the Reflector. We further develop EvoTIDE, a training pipeline that recovers usable trajectories through edit extraction and prefix continuation, then combines SFT with interleaved GRPO across the two roles. Extensive experiments across three coding benchmarks demonstrate that Evo$^2$ significantly outperforms existing self-evolution methods. It achieves 82.1% on Polyglot and 48.3% on SWE-bench Verified, compared with 62.6% and 41.0% for the strongest baseline, respectively. We also show that the evolved harnesses transfer to different tasks without further evolution and rank first in cross-benchmark evaluations. Our dual-role harness improvement framework is also able to extend to self-evolution with proprietary models, improving a GPT-5-mini agent's performance from 24.4% to 48.3%. These results demonstrate the applicability of the framework Evo$^2$ across domains and its broad transferability across models and tasks.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Post-Quantum Session Establishment for Matter over Thread: Message Size, Transport, and Protocol Options
item.description: arXiv:2610.13026v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Matter's first post-quantum change protects device attestation with ML-DSA, but its operational handshake, CASE, still derives session keys from P-256 ECDH, so recorded traffic can be decrypted once a quantum computer exists. We quantify the cost of moving CASE to ML-KEM and post-quantum signatures over Thread, where frames carry at most 127 bytes and a Matter message at most 1178 bytes. A byte-exact model of the CASE messages shows that a drop-in ML-KEM-768/ML-DSA-44 handshake grows from 1.6 kB to 22.8 kB and that no fully post-quantum configuration built from FIPS 203/204/205 algorithms fits the message limit. A Monte Carlo model of multi-hop Thread, calibrated to OpenThread and Matter source constants, shows that sending these messages as fragmented IPv6 datagrams causes spurious retransmissions whenever a message and its reply outlast Matter's retransmission timer. At three to four hops the drop-in handshake then takes 1.8 to 2.6 times longer than with a selective-repeat block transfer, with or without interference, and up to 33% of handshakes with sleepy devices fail; raising the timers does not remove the effect. Caching certificate chains and authenticating the device with a pre-distributed ML-KEM key reduce the handshake to 6.1 kB and 44 ms of device computation. As a first step, hybrid P-256+ML-KEM-512 key exchange with a cached device chain protects session keys against harvest-now, decrypt-later attacks while every message still fits the current limit.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Dataset-Specific Encoding of Image Content Underlies Cross-Dataset Failure in Brain MRI Foundation Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.13027v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Frozen features of brain MRI foundation models lose accuracy on new datasets, a failure usually blamed on the features encoding where each scan came from. We show that the failure lies elsewhere. Across 17 public datasets and eight frozen representations, every representation recognizes the MRI sequence within each dataset, yet most fail on an unseen one. The cause is neither dataset encoding nor a shift of each dataset: the content itself is encoded along different directions in each dataset. This explains which datasets fail, for the sequence and for sex, and why removing the dataset signal with INLP, LEACE, CORAL or adversarial training never improves sequence transfer. Only the broadly pretrained 3DINO and SAM-Med3D encode the sequence consistently enough to transfer; the brain-specific BrainIAC and BrainFM do no better than an untrained network. Code is available at https://github.com/BrainFM/brainfm-profiler/tree/main/representation_utility.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Low-Rank Kolmogorov-Arnold Generator Flows for Interpretable Operator Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.13028v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural operators that learn physical laws from data should generalize beyond their training distribution and expose the learned law in closed form. The Kolmogorov-Arnold neural operator achieves both for position-dependent dynamics by learning a dense pseudo-differential symbol over all positions and frequencies, at a cost that grows with the square of the resolution and with closed forms that must be read out by hand. This dense symbol is unnecessary: a finite-order variable-coefficient differential operator has a symbol whose separation rank is bounded by the number of its coefficient functions, independently of the resolution, and the symbols that this network learns on its own benchmarks have rank two. We introduce the Kolmogorov-Arnold flow (KAFlow), which learns the generator of a physical operator as a low-rank symbol built from univariate Kolmogorov-Arnold functions, fixes the gauge of these functions so that every term has a unique place, integrates the dynamics with exact exponential integrators, and distills its closed form automatically. On the synthetic benchmarks of the Kolmogorov-Arnold neural operator, KAFlow lowers the out-of-distribution loss by 3.4 to 11 times and recovers every coefficient to within 10^-4 without symbolic templates, reaching the precision floor of the data. On long-horizon quantum dynamics, it lowers the state infidelity by up to 6 orders of magnitude, and by 30 times when trained only on position and momentum measurements. KAFlow also learns a variable-order fractional operator 15 times more accurately than existing operator networks and discovers nonlocal, fractional and non-polynomial dispersion relations on which sparse regression fails.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Linear and entropy-stable scheme for the dynamic van der Waals model of non-isothermal liquid-vapor flows
item.description: arXiv:2610.13029v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we propose a linear and decoupled fully discrete scheme that preserves the entropy production property for the dynamic van der Waals model. This model provides a thermodynamically consistent diffuse-interface framework for describing non-isothermal phase transitions in single-component liquid-vapor systems, containing the coupled conservation laws of mass, momentum and energy. We first introduce an equivalent reformulation of the governing equations that avoids the use of chain-rule identities, which generally fail under discrete differentiation. Further, a component-wise convex-splitting method is employed to calculate the discrete chemical potential and temperature. This treatment provides a discrete entropy-stable inequality without a time step restriction. Based on the explicitly treated velocity, the scheme allows the three conservation equations to be solved linearly and sequentially in a decoupled manner. Since the momentum equation does not directly affect the entropy-stability analysis, we use a classical linear semi-implicit scheme to solve it. Numerical experiments verify the expected numerical accuracy. Simulations of droplet evaporation and two- and three-dimensional Leidenfrost effects further demonstrate the proposed method can capture complex non-isothermal phase-transition dynamics while numerically reproducing the discrete entropy production behavior.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Beyond Hypercontractivity: Stronger Communication Converses via R\'enyi Contraction
item.description: arXiv:2610.13030v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the relationship between strong data-processing inequalities for R\'enyi divergences and hypercontractivity. For R\'enyi divergences of order greater than one, we characterize the contraction of R\'enyi divergences through a property of the dual Markov operator that we name power contraction. Using the contraction coefficient, we derive an upper bound on rectangle probabilities in terms of their marginals that is at least as strong as the corresponding bound obtained via hypercontractivity. Combining this result with inversion of the binary R\'enyi divergence, we derive communication lower bounds for one-way communication-assisted agreement distillation. Examples involving binary symmetric and rare-event Z-channels illustrate the improvements over standard hypercontractive converses.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Virtual Transmission Lines from Data Center Workload Migration: Coordinated Multi-Year Transmission Expansion Planning
item.description: arXiv:2610.13032v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid growth of electricity demand from AI data centers is creating a dual mismatch in power systems: a temporal mismatch between fast-rising demand and slow transmission expansion, and a spatial mismatch between concentrated data-center loads and geographically dispersed renewable resources. These mismatches can exacerbate transmission congestion, resulting in unserved data-center load and renewable-energy curtailment. This study models geographic workload migration as a virtual transmission line (VTL) that changes nodal data-center demand without transferring physical electricity. A mixed-integer linear programming model is then developed to co-optimize multi-year candidate-line construction and workload migration, subject to construction delays, renewable-energy curtailment, unserved data-center load, workload-balance requirements, communication-bandwidth constraints, and link-latency limits. The model is evaluated over an eight-year planning horizon on a modified IEEE 14-bus system. The results show that coordinating VTL with physical transmission expansion reduces total system cost, unserved data-center load, and renewable-energy curtailment while alleviating transmission congestion. VTL-aware planning also requires one fewer candidate line than build-only planning. However, VTL alone cannot meet system demand and does not eliminate the need for physical transmission reinforcement. Sensitivity analysis indicates that VTL provides the greatest value when transfer capacity is tight, construction costs are high, load growth is rapid, and data-center flexibility is greater. Additional validation on the IEEE 118-bus system over a five-year planning horizon shows that coordinated planning retains its cost and reliability benefits while reducing physical expansion requirements.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] GeoGR: Spatial-Semantic Token Compression and Group Routing for Efficient 3D VLMs
item.description: arXiv:2610.13035v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-view representations enable pretrained image and video vision-language models to understand 3D scenes, but their long visual token sequences make inference costly. Redundancy arises both from repeated observations of the same scene regions across views and from processing all visual tokens at every LLM layer, regardless of their relevance to the current computation. We propose GeoGR, a two-stage framework that jointly compresses scene representations and visual computation. At the projector level, GeoSemZip consolidates cross-view observations into 3D voxel tokens and combines semantic saliency with spatial coverage to construct a compact scene representation. Unselected voxel features are aggregated into contextual anchors to retain scene information that would otherwise be discarded. At the LLM level, we identify an effective visual computation window and observe that query-conditioned token relevance remains locally stable but changes over longer layer intervals. Guided by these findings, GroupRoute combines late entry and early exit with recoverable group-wise skipping. Low-relevance tokens bypass complete LLM layers while retaining their hidden states and can rejoin the active group at subsequent anchor layers selected under a computation budget. For compression-aware post-training, we construct a compact dataset of 67K samples by retaining 30% of the original training pool. With this protocol, GeoGR retains 95.2% and 96.8% of the dense post-trained models' performance on LLaVA-OneVision-7B and Video-3D LLM-7B, respectively, while accelerating LLM prefill by $6.8\times$ and $6.1\times$. These results demonstrate the consistent effectiveness of GeoGR across 3D VLMs with and without explicit 3D spatial encoding, highlighting a favorable performance-efficiency trade-off. The code is available at https://github.com/EIT-NLP/GeoGR.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Towards Easier-to-Tune Training Algorithms: New Results from AlgoPerf
item.description: arXiv:2610.13036v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evaluating deep learning optimizer is challenging because confounding factors such as hyperparameter tuning and optimizer-model co-design often obscure true algorithmic performance. We present results of the updated AlgoPerf V1 benchmark, in which we evaluate a new set of training algorithms on wall-clock time-to-target across nine workloads on fixed hardware. This report focuses on the results of the benchmark's self-tuning ruleset, which requires submissions to use a single configuration across all workloads. Out of the 13 submissions in PyTorch and JAX, Schedule-Free AdamW ranked first. In addition to the wall-clock scores, we also analyze the trade-offs between step efficiency and wall-clock execution, revealing that matrix-preconditioned and two-loop methods achieve good sample efficiency but require more aggressive computational optimizations to be competitive in runtime. Finally, our hyperparameter saliency and retention analyses show that the learning rate and momentum are highly sensitive across domains and algorithms, highlighting the need for methods that are more robust against hyperparameter tuning and can generalize well to new tasks.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] RAMP: Recurrent Adaptive Mixed Precision for Efficient Prefill in Recurrent-Depth Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.13041v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recurrent-depth language models improve inference-time reasoning by repeatedly applying a shared network to refine internal representations, but the additional recurrent computation also increases inference cost. This overhead is particularly pronounced during long-context prefill, where the full input sequence is repeatedly processed across recurrent depth. Weight-and-activation quantization offers a natural way to accelerate this computation through lower-precision arithmetic, yet repeatedly applying quantized computation introduces numerical perturbations that accumulate along the recurrent trajectory. We systematically analyze how such errors propagate across recurrent depth and show that quantization errors introduced earlier are attenuated by more subsequent recurrent steps and therefore have a smaller effect on the final representation. Matched-budget experiments strongly support this prediction, showing that placing quantized computation earlier in recurrent depth consistently yields the best fidelity. Based on this insight, we introduce RAMP (Recurrent Adaptive Mixed Precision), which performs early recurrent refinement using low-precision weight-and-activation computation and restores high precision for terminal refinement. Across context lengths up to 4K, RAMP preserves near-full-precision prefill quality while achieving up to 1.16x end-to-end first-prefill speedup on an NVIDIA H100, corresponding to a 13.9% latency reduction.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Provably Subexponential Algorithms for Bounded-Error LWE with Few Samples
item.description: arXiv:2610.13043v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that a variant of the Wagner/BKW-style algorithm for LWE of Kirchner and Fouque [KF15] solves decision and search LWE with secrets of size $n$ over prime moduli $q=n^{\kappa+o(1)}$, for any fixed $\kappa>0$, with errors bounded by $\exp((\ln n)^{o(1)})$, in time $2^{O(n/\ln\ln n)}$ given $n+O(n/\ln\ln n)$ original samples. Further, if each coordinate of the secret is also bounded by $\exp((\ln n)^{o(1)})$, the same time bound holds with errors bounded by $n^{o(1)}$ and only $O(n/\ln\ln q)$ samples. Earlier, it was known that Kirchner and Fouque's algorithm could solve LWE with these parameters in subexponential time with a much larger number of samples $m = \Omega(n\log{n})$ [HKM18]. Ducas et al. [DEL25] showed that an adaptation of this algorithm could solve the corresponding dual, the $\mathrm{SIS}^{\infty}$ problem, with a suitable norm bound $q/\operatorname{polylog}(n)$ and $m=n+\omega(n/\ln\ln n)$ variables in subexponential time. Whereas their analysis involves interpreting the algorithm in terms of chains of lattices, our approach is quite elementary and is based on bounding the lower moments of a Fourier statistic.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Redirecting Teacher Supervision: Temporal-Response-Guided Latent Distillation for Video-Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.13045v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers capabilities through teacher predictions on student-generated sequences, as studied by GKD and MiniLLM for language models and Video-OPD for video tasks. We ask how internal supervision can further support temporal learning. Direct hidden-state alignment does not explicitly use the student's temporal responses to choose a supervision direction. We propose Temporal-Response Guidance (TRG), which measures representation responses to local temporal perturbations, adds the teacher correction's projection onto their span back to the original correction, and restores its original norm. The projection is not normalized separately, and correction components outside the response space are retained. With an orthogonal tangent projector and a detached target, TRG changes the supervision direction while preserving the cosine-loss value and aligned-representation gradient norm at target construction. On TempCompass, Video-MME, MVBench, and Video-MMMU, TRG improves the 4B student's macro accuracy by 2.86 percentage points over the reported output-only OPD baseline.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Execution-Feasible Dispatch of LLM Pre-training Loads for Renewable-Dominant AI Data Centers
item.description: arXiv:2610.13047v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI data centers (AIDCs) are emerging as large power-system loads, making their operational flexibility increasingly valuable. Existing studies often treat AIDC demand as continuously adjustable or generically delay-tolerant, which overstating the flexibility of large language model (LLM) pretraining. This paper proposes an execution-feasible dispatch framework for LLM pre-training in renewable-dominant AIDCs. LLM descriptors are first converted into checkpoint-domain daily workloads, then mapped to feasible 3D-parallel GPU modes with explicit throughput, GPU-capacity, memory, and IT-power limits. The resulting checkpoint- and mode-constrained load states are embedded into a day-ahead power dispatch model. Case studies on a 2048 GPUs AIDC with two LLaMA pretraining tasks show that checkpoint-aware 3D dispatch reduces operating cost by 20.02% and renewable curtailment from 1.077 to 0.014 MWh relative to fixed continuous training. Related results also show that checkpoint records alone do not create load flexibility,practical grid-interactive flexibility arises from checkpoint waiting combined with execution-feasible 3D-mode compensation.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Failure-Resilient Multi-Robot Coordination with $k$-Connectivity Constrained Submodular Maximization
item.description: arXiv:2610.13049v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-robot coordination is essential in applications such as coverage, target tracking, and information gathering, where robots must jointly select actions to maximize team performance. Submodular maximization provides an effective framework for such coordination, and resilient variants further account for robot failures or adversarial removals. However, existing methods typically overlook the impact of robot loss on the communication network, which may disconnect the surviving team and prevent continued coordination. To address this issue, we introduce Resilient $k$-Connected Submodular Maximization, which jointly considers task performance, resilience, and communication connectivity. The resulting feasible family is not a matroid, preventing the direct application of classical curvature-greedy guarantees. We overcome this challenge through a Menger-based connectivity reduction, a connectivity-aware greedy algorithm with a feasibility-preserving fallback, and a new curvature-based analysis that captures the cost of enforcing connectivity through a single factor $\rho$. Our method achieves a worst-case post-failure objective within a factor of $[\max(1-\nu_f(\mathcal{I}),h(N,\beta))]^2 \rho \frac{1}{\kappa_f}(1-e^{-\kappa_f})$ of the optimal connectivity-respecting resilient assignment, while recovering the classical unconstrained guarantee in the appropriate limits. Experiments on multi-robot target tracking validate the proposed method and characterize the practical impact of connectivity constraints.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] NOFACE3D: NOise-scheduled Focused Anchoring and Controlled Enhancement for 3D Generation
item.description: arXiv:2610.13050v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent image-to-3D models generate complete, high-quality assets from a single image, with global shape and appearance that are already convincing; what remains is the fine scale, where small, thin, elongated, or detail-rich regions are reconstructed softly and under-resolved. This gap can arise in generators with fixed-resolution spatial grids: the same spatial sampling density is used for a large, smooth, low-curvature surface and for a thin, high-curvature structure that carries most of the perceived detail. To this end, we introduce NOFACE3D, a training-free framework that refines these detail-critical regions while preserving the rest of the asset. Given a generated mesh, its input image, and a refinement box, NOFACE3D extracts the selected submesh, scales it up to fill the generator's input volume, and re-encodes it into the full-resolution latent grid. Conditioned on the image crop, it refines the region through flow-based sampling with a spatially varying noise schedule that anchors boundary latents. The refined region is then integrated back into the original asset, preserving the surrounding geometry and appearance. We implement NOFACE3D on TRELLIS.2 and its sparse voxel representation; all of it operates purely at inference time on the frozen pretrained generator. We evaluate NOFACE3D on PAniC-3D, TexVerse and BigDetail, a new benchmark of 339 assets with annotated detail-critical regions. On all three, it generates sharper geometry and finer texture detail than the baselines. Project page: https://idkcouscous.github.io/NoFACE3D/
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Space Over Statistic, Retraining Over Ranking: Auditing Training Labels Under Label-Only Backdoors
item.description: arXiv:2610.13051v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Some backdoor attacks never touch an image. FLIP only changes labels: on CIFAR-10, flipping 3% of them makes a ResNet-32 send 99.7% of triggered source-class images to the attacker's class. The usual defenses look for the poison inside a model trained on those same labels. So when they struggle, is the problem the test they run, or the space they run it in? We answer with a controlled swap: we keep the test, the labels and the metric fixed, change only the feature space, and judge each defense by retraining the victim on what it keeps. The space decides. On dog$\to$cat the same nearest-neighbor check scores AUROC 0.546 on the poisoned model's features, 0.967 on frozen DINOv2 features that never saw a label, and 0.995 on the same network trained on clean labels, an oracle control rather than a defense. We reproduce SPECTRE, the defense FLIP's authors recommend, to 90.94 / 0.97 against its published 91.47 / 1.7, then price it: on truck$\to$deer it deletes 20% of every class, while a prototype audit on the frozen features deletes 6% for higher clean accuracy and lower attack success. On three harder pairs that audit leaves about a quarter of the attack standing. A count read off encoder geometry and clean labels, before any attack is run, separates the pair where the audit removes the attack from those where it only partly does, though on a single zero-count pair. Three results warn against the easy story. A better detection score does not mean a safer model: on two of four pairs Confident Learning scores the higher AUROC, and on dog$\to$cat leaves 2.6 times the attack success. The prototype family, our best static performer, is the first an adaptive attacker slips past. And past a point, catching more poisons stops reducing attack success. Check labels in a space that never learned them, and judge a defense by the retrained model, not by its detection score.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] UniMergeTrack: Hierarchical Model Merging for General RGB-X Visual Object Tracking
item.description: arXiv:2610.13053v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: RGB-X tracking leverages complementary modalities, such as thermal infrared, event, or depth, to improve robustness under challenging conditions. Existing general-purpose RGB-X trackers typically follow two paradigms: independent task-specific training and joint training across modality combinations. However, the former suffers from knowledge isolation and model redundancy, while the latter introduces optimization interference across heterogeneous tasks. In this work, we present UniMergeTrack, a new model merging paradigm that preserves task-specific optimization while enabling effective cross-task knowledge integration. UniMergeTrack first trains modality-specific trackers independently and then performs hierarchical model merging. Specifically, transferable backbones are merged across RGB-X tasks via high-pass-filtered merging, and complemented by lightweight task-specific experts that preserve modality-specific cues. Tracking heads are merged within each task using optimal transport-guided channel alignment to mitigate hidden channel mismatch. A subsequent distribution alignment fine-tuning stage further improves compatibility between the unified backbone and task-specific heads. Extensive experiments on the LasHeR, RGBT234, VisEvent, VOT-RGBD22, COESOT, and CDTB benchmarks demonstrate that UniMergeTrack achieves state-of-the-art or competitive performance across RGB-Thermal, RGB-Event, and RGB-Depth tracking tasks, while exhibiting strong generalization to unseen datasets. The source code will be released upon acceptance. The source code of this paper will be released on https://github.com/Event-AHU/OpenEvTracking.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] LiveSynth: A Streaming Neural Synthesizer for Instrument Cloning and Text-to-Instrument
item.description: arXiv:2610.13054v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recently, generative neural synthesizers have enabled zero-shot instrument cloning from reference recordings and timbre generation from text prompts. However, existing systems generate complete audio segments offline, precluding their use as playable instruments. We present LiveSynth, a streaming neural synthesizer with flexible timbre control and interactive generation capabilities, including zero-shot instrument cloning and text-to-instrument synthesis. A feedback-free causal Transformer conditioned on MIDI events and a CLAP timbre embedding outputs continuous audio latents at 100 Hz, which a causal variational autoencoder decodes into audio. Frame-wise timbre conditioning enables continuous timbre morphing, while MIDI-conditioning dropout enables autonomous continuation from a performed prefix. On the NSynth and Slakh datasets, LiveSynth achieved timbre similarity and spectral reconstruction quality comparable to offline baselines. On an M3 MacBook Air, LiveSynth required 8.8 ms of computation per 10 ms audio frame (an RTF of 0.88) with 10 ms algorithmic latency, enabling real-time interaction with a performer.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] A4-MR: Abnormality-aware Anatomical Alignment for MR
item.description: arXiv:2610.13056v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in large-scale foundation models have enabled strong generalization across a wide range of clinical and research tasks in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). However, existing vision-language MRI models remain limited in anatomy-specific localization and pathology-aware representation, particularly in real-world settings. We introduce A4-MR, a 3D vision-language foundation model trained on approximately 50,000 MRI studies comprising 491,000 series, roughly half of which are paired with radiology reports. A4-MR is designed to: (1) learn anatomy localization through large-scale pretraining with noisy labels; (2) align image and text representations at the anatomical level; and (3) learn distinct representations of healthy and abnormal anatomy. Across a diverse set of downstream tasks, A4-MR outperforms existing foundation models, including a +1.7 AUROC improvement over MedSigLIP for abnormality detection. Using a frozen encoder, A4-MR also surpasses an end-to-end task-specific MedNeXt model for knee segmentation by +1.4 Dice and performs comparably to the best task-specific model for abdominal organ segmentation on AMOS, within 0.4 Dice. Finally, without anatomical prompts, A4-MR localizes 3D anatomy comparably to MedSAM2 provided with ground-truth bounding boxes. Together, these results demonstrate that anatomy-level multimodal alignment and abnormality-aware representation learning can enable a single MRI foundation model to support localization, segmentation, and pathology-related tasks.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] CoBe: A Benchmark For Conversational Counterfactual Text Editing
item.description: arXiv:2610.13057v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Counterfactual text editing is the ability to revise a given text in light of a hypothetical change while preserving facts not causally affected by that change. When asked what would have happened if a doctor had not recommended surgery, the model output should retain the patient's medical history and modify only the consequences of the decision. This requires causal understanding: a model must determine, without being explicitly instructed to, what events are affected by the hypothetical change and what should remain fixed. This skill is central to human reasoning, especially in safety-critical domains like healthcare or law. By contrast, the task of associational text generation merely generates text statistically associated with the altered condition. In the medical example, an associational response might make the patient's symptoms less severe because milder cases correlate with no surgery. Such responses produce a plausible scenario, but not the counterfactual version of the given one. Prior counterfactual-text datasets do not clearly separate these modes of reasoning. We introduce the Counterfactual Benchmark (CoBe), a testbed for models' zero-shot ability to counterfactually edit a given textual scenario when prompted to do so in a conversationally natural way. CoBe contains 2000 questions spanning healthcare, science and engineering, business, and everyday scenarios. We test a suite of frontier and smaller models, with frontier systems achieving an average score of $58.05\%$. Our findings indicate that models frequently default to associational generation rather than preserving the causal structure of the original scenario. Moreover, performance does not scale consistently with either model size or output token length, suggesting that the failure may reflect model training objectives rather than insufficient model capacity.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Travel Back To Move Forward: Retrospective Exploration and Evolving for Long Horizon Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.13058v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model agents increasingly operate in long-horizon environments where early mistakes can trigger cascading failures and trap agents in dead-end trajectories. Agents must therefore be able to proactively recover from such states and turn their exploratory experience into guidance for subsequent decisions. We introduce ReTRAIL, a framework that enables agents to rewind the environment to earlier states while preserving valid progress and carrying forward knowledge learned from abandoned exploration. The environment state moves backward while the agent's knowledge continues to move forward. ReTRAIL trains a shared policy with two complementary signals: State-Anchored GRPO compares alternative continuations from revisited states to improve execution, while a branch-advancement reward guides reflection through the progress of subsequent exploration. Experiments across four interactive benchmark MineSweeper, Sokoban, ALFWorld and ScienceWorld show that simply adding a rewind primitive provides limited benefit and can even degrade performance. In contrast, ReTRAIL enables agents to rewind from unproductive states and use insights from abandoned branches to guide subsequent exploration. These results demonstrate the value of coupling environment rewinding with experience reuse within an ongoing task for long-horizon task solving. The code is available at https://github.com/whi497/ReTRAIL.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] CliQ-RRG: Clinical-Knowledge Guided Disease-aware Visual-Textual Alignment for QA-Style Radiology Report Generation
item.description: arXiv:2610.13059v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Radiology reports are essential for diagnostic reasoning and patient care, yet their manual preparation is time-consuming and cognitively demanding. Automatic radiology report generation (RRG) offers a scalable alternative, but existing models often produce lengthy, unstructured narratives that overlook diagnostic cues and multi-view information. We present Clinical-Knowledge Guided Disease-aware Visual-Textual Alignment for QA-Style Radiology Report Generation (CliQ-RRG), a unified two-stage framework for interpretable and clinically grounded reporting. In Stage 1, CliQ-RRG employs a Disease-aware Visual-Textual Alignment module that aligns image and text representations using predicted disease embeddings, reinforced by a Prior-Guided Attention Module (PrAM) to capture multi-view dependencies across current and prior scans. In Stage 2, GraphRAG-guided retrieval augments intermediate textual representations with graph-grounded clinical evidence, and a large language model restructures them into concise, interpretable question-answer (QA) pairs with diagnostic summaries. Experiments on two public chest X-ray benchmarks demonstrate that CliQ-RRG consistently outperforms prior methods across both lexical and clinical metrics, generating accurate and clinically coherent QA-style radiology reports. Code is available at: https://github.com/chandravardhan-singh-raghaw/CliQ-RRG.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] KV-Repurpose: A Testbed for Evaluating Non-Prefix KV-Cache Reuse
item.description: arXiv:2610.13060v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: KV-cache reuse in large language model serving is commonly limited to exact prompt prefixes, preventing reuse when the same retrieved document appears after different system prompts, conversation histories, or dynamic metadata. We present KV-Repurpose, an open-source, vLLM-based system for developing and evaluating segment-wise KV-cache reuse beyond exact prefixes. The system combines cache-aware segment scheduling, prompt construction, capacity management, workload generation, and runtime monitoring. Experiments on long-context benchmarks show that naive segment reuse largely preserves output quality for single-document question answering and summarization, while exposing clear limitations in cross-document reasoning. Under a Zipfian RAG-style workload in which 20% of requests share a fixed prefix, KV-Repurpose achieves a substantially higher token-level cache hit rate than prefix caching at the same 30 GB cache capacity, 63.9% versus 3.3%, resulting in lower TTFT. Even with 1 TB of cache capacity, prefix caching reaches only a 17.9% hit rate in this workload. Source code is available under the Apache-2.0 license at https://github.com/taiga333/eval-kv-repurpose.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Capturing Electrical Windows Through Reconfigurable Optical Networks: Transfer-aware Scheduling of Multi-Region AI Data Centers
item.description: arXiv:2610.13061v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artificial-intelligence data centers (AIDCs) can provide spatiotemporal load flexibility by migrating training workloads in response to regional electricity prices and renewable-energy (RE) availability. However, transfer-blind scheduling may overestimate migration benefits by overlooking transfer time or prevent training from resuming within renewable-rich or low-price windows when considering transfer time. This paper proposes a transfer-aware compute-electricity-network scheduling framework that coordinates training placement, checkpoint transmission, and optical circuit switching (OCS) to improve local RE utilization and reduce grid-purchase cost. A compact compute-electricity master problem generates candidate schedules using estimated transfer delays. The framework then schedules optical circuits, verifies checkpoint delivery under shared-link capacity constraints, and revises infeasible schedules using updated delay estimates. It integrates day-ahead planning, event-triggered intraday updates, and real-time dispatch. In a five-AIDC benchmark with equal completed work and network resources, the proposed method reduces the real-time grid purchase cost by 12.50% and increases the local RE utilization by 2.724 percentage points relative to static optical operation. Sensitivity and ablation analyses indicate that OCS is particularly beneficial when renewable-rich or low-price windows shift across sites and network bottlenecks hinder timely checkpoint delivery.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] CB-Orchestrator: Adaptive Workflow Optimization for LLM Agents via Contextual Bandits
item.description: arXiv:2610.13064v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in tackling complex tasks through agentic workflows. However, manually designing these workflows is labor-intensive and lacks flexibility to adapt to diverse queries. While automated workflow optimization is a promising direction, existing methods often incur expensive API costs during training-phase feedback collection. Furthermore, they fail to adaptively reuse high-quality workflows, which creates a bottleneck for both performance and cost-effectiveness. To address these limitations, we propose CB-Orchestrator, an adaptive framework that decouples workflow generation from selection. In the first stage, we construct a diverse pool of candidate workflows via evolutionary search. In the second stage, we formulate workflow selection as a Contextual Bandit problem, which enables sample-efficient learning by balancing exploration and exploitation, thereby significantly reducing the feedback required for training. During inference, the model adaptively selects the optimal workflow tailored to each query. Evaluations across five diverse benchmarks demonstrate that CB-Orchestrator consistently outperforms all baselines. Notably, on the MATH dataset, CB-Orchestrator achieves better performance than strong recent baselines while reducing training-phase API token overhead by no less than 40.55% and total end-to-end training (including workflow pool generation) token overhead by no less than 29.73%.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] TestSuiteBench: Coding Agents Struggle to Generate Strong Test Suites from Specifications
item.description: arXiv:2610.13065v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coding agents are increasingly used to create large software projects. While code-generation benchmarks have scaled accordingly to full applications, test-generation benchmarks remain limited to individual functions or bug fixes. In particular, generating complete test suites for complex software from scratch remains unexplored. To address this gap, we introduce TestSuiteBench, a benchmark of 165 open-source applications, each with a structured and detailed specification of intended behavior, a reference implementation, a reference test suite, and on average 74 mutants. Each mutant is generated from a single requirement of the specification and refined to isolate that behavior: 73\% are killed by exactly one reference test and, on average, by only 0.2\% of the remaining tests. We find that even frontier coding agents struggle to generate strong test suites given our specifications, achieving mutation scores below 60\%, despite their suites being largely valid and 88\% of their tests passing on the reference implementation. We observe that generated test suites often lack relevant input combinations and are smaller than reference test suites. Meanwhile, implementations generated for the same specifications pass 82\% of the reference tests. These results show agents can build software they cannot verify, a gap that directly limits fully autonomous software development.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Evolving Creatives with Clicks: CTR-Driven Advertising image Editing via Attribute Disentanglement and Preference Alignment
item.description: arXiv:2610.13066v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The optimization objective for e-commerce advertising creatives has shifted from aesthetic quality to online business metrics like click-through rate (CTR). Recent methods generate appealing ad images from product images by constructing CTR-based reward signals and refining prompt generation via Reinforcement Learning. Such paradigms equally penalize all attributes within an underperforming image, even though some are actually beneficial to clicks. In this work, we propose Evolving Creatives with Clicks (ECC), which reformulates creative optimization as fine-grained editing rather than generation from scratch. ECC selectively refines attributes that hurt CTR while preserving those that contribute positively. Specifically, faced with a rich attribute space across massive images, ECC first identifies 28 attributes significantly correlated with CTR via ANOVA and Random Forest regression. Based on attribute contrasts between images with disparate CTRs, we instruction-tune a prompt model to generate editing suggestions, then refine it with real click preferences since reference-derived suggestions are not uniformly beneficial. Furthermore, we introduce Consistent Preference Optimization (CPO) as ECC's preference optimization strategy, which enforces consistency across semantically equivalent shuffled suggestions to mitigate DPO overfitting and improve preference generalization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ECC significantly improves the CTR of ad images, outperforming state-of-the-art models by a substantial margin. The complete data pipeline, including attribute extraction and analysis, the resulting dataset, and source code will be released upon acceptance.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] TPCS: A Cycle-Level Simulation Paradigm with Native Execution Semantics for RTL Modeling and Generation
item.description: arXiv:2610.13067v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The growing diversity of domain-specific architectures and microarchitectural designs demands fast and accurate evaluation methods during early design stages. However, existing approaches suffer from a fundamental trade-off: high-level simulators offer speed but lack fidelity, while RTL-based tools provide accuracy at the cost of significant simulation overhead. This gap limits efficient pre-RTL microarchitecture exploration. Therefore, we propose Transaction-Pruned Cycle Simulation (TPCS), a novel modeling and simulation framework. It serves as a unified intermediate abstraction spanning microarchitecture modeling, cycle-accurate simulation, and synthesizable RTL implementation. TPCS organizes combinational logic as transaction-based function invocations and leverages host CPU control flow to naturally prune inactive logic, eliminating the need for explicit event scheduling or signal tracking. This enables cycle-accurate simulation with significantly improved performance. TPCS preserves structural correspondence with RTL and supports automatic generation of synthesizable designs. TPCS achieves 36$\times$-42$\times$ speedups over parallel Verilator on SMP systems and 3.4$\times$-7.2$\times$ over single-threaded Verilator on accelerators, with cycle-level waveform agreement on the evaluated traces. The generated RTL demonstrates comparable timing and area to handcrafted implementations, with relative changes of -4.7\% to +2.6\% in clock period and -3.3\% to +4.0\% in standard-cell area. By bridging the abstraction gap between high-level modeling and RTL design, TPCS enables a unified and agile pre-RTL workflow, allowing efficient microarchitecture exploration with both high performance and implementation fidelity.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] CAPE - Context-Aware Prioritization Engine for Vulnerability Scoring and Management
item.description: arXiv:2610.13071v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vulnerability patching is critical for safeguarding an enterprise's software ecosystem from cyber attacks. However, patching requires adequate preparation for potential system downtime and for unforeseen effects of the patched software on a live system. Thus, effective risk mitigation requires prioritization strategies that explicitly account for the operational context of the affected software. While vulnerability prioritization based on Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS), Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS) and CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, can help, their differing goals and methodologies often lead to inconsistent, context-unaware decisions resulting in mis-allocated remediation efforts. In this work, we present the Context-Aware Prioritization Engine (CAPE), a vulnerability analysis framework that enriches each vulnerability scanner report of vulnerabilities (CVEs) with deployment-specific evidence. This evidence is used to perform vulnerability reachability, centrality, and exploitability analysis, producing a ranked priority score for the effective distribution of remediation effort. We evaluate CAPE on 30 open-source agentic applications comprising 6,138 scanner-reported CVEs. Our evaluation shows that a significant majority of CVEs are not reachable and exploitable which results in significant disparities between CAPE and context-free baselines - the CVSS, EPSS, and KEV. It also shows that CAPE consistently surfaces confirmed-exploitable CVEs at higher priority than all baselines, demonstrating that context-aware analysis provides substantially more accurate remediation guidance than context-free severity scoring alone.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] AV-FlowEdit: Training-Free Prompt-Driven Audio-Visual Editing with Event-Aware Spectral Trajectory Preservation
item.description: arXiv:2610.13072v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Joint audio-video diffusion models generate synchronized content, but editing existing clips requires target changes without disrupting non-target structure or cross-modal correspondence. We present AV-FlowEdit, a training-free and inversion-free framework for prompt-driven audio-video editing. Our key insight is that source--target flow differences provide both cross-modal editing directions and preservation cues. Under shared perturbations, they jointly update the video and audio branches, supporting visual-only, audio-only, and joint edits while retaining pretrained cross-modal interactions. To suppress drift accumulated during sampling, Cross-Modal Event-Aware Spectral Trajectory Preservation combines flow saliency, aligned audio activity, multiscale low-frequency displacement, and diffusion-stage scheduling. This adaptively preserves unsupported regions while allowing intended audio-visual events. AV-FlowEdit requires no model training, external masks, or optimization-based inversion. Experiments show strong prompt alignment and temporal consistency, together with competitive audio quality and cross-modal coherence.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Double-Take: Improving Capacity, Binding, and Selectivity In Long-Context Within Bidirectional Memory
item.description: arXiv:2610.13073v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Processing a long sequence does not guarantee that distant information remains usable. As context grows, a fixed-size memory must retain many associations, connect information across positions, and preserve relevant structure without being overwhelmed by everything it observes. These are distinct requirements: a memory may store more information without representing the relationships needed for retrieval, and it may transport those relationships without preserving the ones that matter. Thus, the challenge is not simply extending context length, but constructing a memory that remains usable as context grows. We study this problem in large-chunk test-time training (TTT) and identify two basic failures: single-step writes accumulate interference, limiting capacity, while self-associative writes cannot form cross-position bindings. We introduce Double-Take (DT), which repairs these failures with multi-step unpinned updates and cross-position mixing, and adds bidirectional change-sensitive writes for selective retention. Capacity alone leaves end-to-end recall at the $0.10$ chance floor; adding binding raises it to $0.92$. Trained only on $32\,\mathrm{kb}$ genomic contexts, DT reaches $0.927$ AUROC at $131\,\mathrm{kb}$ and $0.856$ near $1\,\mathrm{Mb}$, while transferring zero-shot from human to mouse. Together, these results identify capacity, binding, and selectivity as three requirements for usable long-range memory.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] LongHarness: Advancing Agentic Reasoning over 100M-Token Corpora via Stateful Evidence Management
item.description: arXiv:2610.13075v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Corpus-level long-context reasoning requires agents to acquire and integrate evidence across document collections that exceed their context windows. Existing agent harnesses enable incremental access to these corpora, but acquired evidence and evolving conclusions often remain entangled in a growing interaction history. This implicit state management can lead to two coupled failure modes: unbounded exploration, where retrieval expands the interaction history without resolving decision-relevant information gaps, and evidence-state drift, where previously acquired evidence or subsequent corrections fail to inform the current conclusion. We present LongHarness, a model-agnostic harness that makes the interaction between acquired evidence and evolving conclusions explicit. Its core mechanism, Evidence-Conclusion Coevolution, uses unresolved conclusions to guide exploration toward missing information, while newly acquired evidence strengthens or revises the conclusions that directed the search. LongHarness couples this process with Evidence Lifecycle Management, which keeps accumulated evidence current and traceable throughout the interaction. Together, these mechanisms focus retrieval on remaining information needs and keep conclusions aligned with current evidence. We evaluate LongHarness on OfficeQA Pro V1 and V2, AA-LCR, and LongBench v2 using GLM-5.3-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash. Compared with direct reasoning using the same backbone, LongHarness improves GLM-5.3-Flash exact match on OfficeQA Pro from 15.8% to 60.2% on V1 and from 4.4% to 61.1% on V2. Against state-of-the-art agent harnesses, it surpasses Claude Code by 12.0 percentage points on V1 and Codex by 18.9 points on V2. With Qwen3.8-Flash, LongHarness reaches 61.7% on V1, outperforming Claude Code by 8.3 points and Codex by 12.0 points.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org
